content: Herpetic whitlow is a painful lesion that typically occurs on the fingers or thumbs and is caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). In children, the primary source of infection is often the orofacial region, with HSV-1 being the most common strain involved. This is frequently transmitted through behaviors such as thumb-sucking or finger-chewing. In adults, the infection is more commonly associated with HSV-2, often following contact with HSV-2-infected genital areas. Healthcare workers, particularly dentists and medical professionals exposed to oral secretions, are also at increased risk due to occupational exposure to the virus. The condition is most commonly contracted by individuals who are HSV-seronegative, meaning they have not previously been exposed to the virus and lack immunity. In children, herpetic whitlow is often observed in those with primary HSV-1 infections, particularly thumb-sucking children. In adults, it is more frequently seen in individuals aged 20 to 30 following contact with HSV-2-infected genital areas. Herpetic whitlow lesions are painful and can manifest on the fingers, thumbs, or occasionally the toes and nail cuticles. The infection is caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2. For example, if an individual with a cold sore places their finger in their mouth, the virus can be transferred, leading to a herpetic whitlow lesion. This condition is also commonly observed among dental professionals, such as dentists and dental hygienists, due to their increased exposure to the herpes virus. The natural course of herpetic whitlow typically involves spontaneous healing within two to three weeks. Symptoms include swelling, redness, and tenderness of the affected finger, which may be accompanied by fever and swollen lymph nodes. On physical examination, small, clear vesicles initially form on the skin, which may later merge and become cloudy. The associated pain is often disproportionate to the visible physical symptoms. In children, herpetic whitlow may follow an earlier episode of herpes gingivostomatitis, while in adults, vesiculobullous lesions on the fingers are characteristic of the condition. Treatment for herpetic whitlow is primarily supportive, as it is a self-limiting illness. However, topical antiviral medications, particularly acyclovir, have been shown to effectively reduce the duration of symptoms. It is crucial to avoid lancing or surgically debriding the lesion, as this can worsen the condition by causing superinfection or even encephalitis.
